extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan), scholars studying sovereignty and early modern political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Hobbes' criteria and standards for what constitutes a commonwealth and sovereign power (generation, definition, rights, and limits) as laid out in Leviathan. Focuses on the institutional features and practical consequences Hobbes gives for recognizing and evaluating sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation Of A Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to erect such a Common Power ... is, to conferre all their power and strength upon one Man, or upon one Assembly of men, that may reduce all their Wills ... unto one Will: which is as much as to say, to appoint one man, or Assembly of men, to beare their Person;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the process by which individuals 'authorize and give up' their right of governing themselves to a representative (one man or an assembly) so that the representative bears their person; every subject must own and acknowledge himself to be author of whatever the representative shall act in matters of common peace and safety. Emphasises that this conferment of power is the sole means to secure defence and civil peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition Of A Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A Common-wealth ... is 'One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author, to the end he may use the strength and means of them all, as he shall think expedient, for their Peace and Common Defence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the canonical definition: the commonwealth consists in the person who represents the united will of the multitude. The definition is the test for recognizing a constituted commonwealth: one representative person whose acts are authorized by the multitude for peace and defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes Of Attaining Sovereign Power
rubrics_metrics.description: The attaining to this Soveraigne Power, is by two wayes. One, by Naturall force ... The other, is when men agree amongst themselves, to submit to some Man, or Assembly of men, voluntarily, on confidence to be protected by him against all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes acquisition of sovereignty by (a) natural force (conquest, subjection) and (b) institution (voluntary covenant). Both modes result in a sovereign who bears the people's person; Hobbes focuses on the instituted commonwealth in the subsequent rights discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects Cannot Change The Forme Of Government
rubrics_metrics.description: They that have already Instituted a Common-wealth ... cannot lawfully make a new Covenant, amongst themselves, to be obedient to any other, in any thing whatsoever, without his permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the institution flows the right that subjects may not, without the sovereign's consent, sever the covenant or transfer their person to another representative; to attempt so is unjust, breaks the original covenant, and leads back to war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Power Cannot Be Forfeited
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Right of bearing the Person of them all, is given ... by Covenant onely of one to another, there can happen no breach of Covenant on the part of the Soveraigne; and consequently none of his Subjects, by any pretence of forfeiture, can be freed from his Subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the sovereign does not enter a reciprocal covenant with subjects and thus cannot forfeit sovereignty by wrongdoing; any claim of forfeiture returns disputes to force, undermining the purpose of the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Man Can Without Injustice Protest Against The Institution Declared By The Major Part
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the major part hath by consenting voices declared a Soveraigne; he that dissented must now consent with the rest ... for he voluntarily entered into the Congregation ... he sufficiently declared thereby his will (and therefore tacitly covenanted) to stand to what the major part should ordayne:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats tacit membership in the original assembly as binding: dissenters who joined cannot legitimately protest decrees of the majority, because their prior presence constituted tacit consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sovereign's Actions Cannot Be Justly Accused By The Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Because every Subject is by this Institution Author of all the Actions, and Judgements of the Soveraigne Instituted; it followes, that whatsoever he doth, it can be no injury to any of his Subjects; nor ought he to be by any of them accused of Injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects are the authors of sovereign acts by virtue of the covenant; therefore complaints of injustice against sovereign actions are incoherent in Hobbes' framework (he distinguishes iniquity from injustice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatsoever The Sovereign Doth, Is Unpunishable By The Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: No man that hath Soveraigne power can justly be put to death, or otherwise in any manner by his Subjects punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subjects are authors of sovereign acts, any punishment by subjects would amount to punishing themselves; this follows from Hobbes' logic about the unity of authorisation and the purpose of avoiding return to the state of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Is Judge Of What Is Necessary For The Peace And Defence
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongeth of Right, to whatsoever Man, or Assembly that hath the Soveraignty, to be Judge both of the meanes of Peace and Defence; and also of the hindrances, and disturbances of the same; and to do whatsoever he shall think necessary to be done ... for the preserving of Peace and Security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign has the right to determine means and measures required for public safety; this includes pre-emptive and remedial actions. The judgment of necessity for peace is vested in the sovereign alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Is Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixtly, it is annexed to the Soveraignty, to be Judge of what Opinions and Doctrines are averse, and what conducing to Peace; and consequently, on what occasions, how farre, and what, men are to be trusted withall, in speaking to Multitudes of people; and who shall examine the Doctrines of all bookes before they be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes censorship and regulation of teaching and publication to the sovereign: doctrine is governed insofar as it affects peace. Hobbes justifies regulating opinion by appeal to prevention of discord and civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right To Prescribe Rules Of Property (Propriety / Meum and Tuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventhly, is annexed to the Soveraigntie, the whole power of prescribing the Rules, whereby every man may know, what Goods he may enjoy and what Actions he may doe ... This Propriety ... is the Act of the Power, in order to the publique peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign authority includes defining private rights and laws of property; these civil laws (meum and tuum) are instruments to prevent war and secure peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of All Judicature And Decision Of Controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Eightly, is annexed to the Soveraigntie, the Right of Judicature; that is to say, of hearing and deciding all Controversies, which may arise concerning Law ... or concerning Fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial power over disputes (civil, natural law, fact) rests with the sovereign; without central decision, private force and war would resume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Making War And Peace; Levying Money; Militia Command
rubrics_metrics.description: Ninthly, is annexed to the Soveraignty, the Right of making Warre, and Peace with other Nations ... and to levy mony upon the Subjects, to defray the expenses thereof. ... the command of the Militia ... maketh him that hath it Soveraigne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign controls external relations, declares war/peace, raises funds, and commands armed forces. Hobbes links military command (militia) directly to sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Choosing All Counsellours, Ministers, And Officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenthly, is annexed to the Soveraigntie, the choosing of all Councellours, Ministers, Magistrates, and Officers, both in peace, and War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign selects the executive and administrative personnel required to discharge duties of governance; this is part of the means to secure the common end of peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Rewarding And Punishing (Arbitrary Where Law Silent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleventhly, to the Soveraigne is committed the Power of Rewarding with riches, or honour; and of Punishing with corporall, or pecuniary punishment, or with ignominy every Subject according to the Lawe he hath formerly made; or if there be no Law made, according as he shall judge most to conduce to the encouraging of men to serve the Common-wealth, or deterring of them from doing dis-service to the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign has distributive and corrective powers; where statutes are absent, sovereign discretion determines measures of reward/punishment to serve public ends (encouragement and deterrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Of Honour And Order (Conferral Of Titles And Dignities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lastly ... It is necessary that there be Lawes of Honour, and a publique rate of the worth of such men as have deserved, or are able to deserve well of the Common-wealth; ... To the Soveraigne therefore it belongeth also to give titles of Honour; and to appoint what Order of place, and dignity, each man shall hold;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign determines public hierarchy, honors, and ceremonial order as instruments to regulate emulation, factions, and preserve peace by formal recognition of status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights Constituting Sovereignty Are Indivisible
rubrics_metrics.description: These are the Rights, which make the Essence of Soveraignty; ... For these are incommunicable, and inseparable. ... if the Soveraign transferre the Militia, he retains the Judicature in vain, for want of execution of the Lawes; ... This division is it, whereof it is said, 'A kingdome divided in it selfe cannot stand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that the bundle of sovereign rights form an indivisible whole: dividing or granting away essential sovereign powers undermines the capacity to secure peace and thereby invalidates the exercise of remaining rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Rights Cannot Pass Away Without Direct Renouncing
rubrics_metrics.description: And because they are essentiall and inseparable Rights, it follows necessarily, that in whatsoever, words any of them seeme to be granted away, yet if the Soveraign Power it selfe be not in direct termes renounced, and the name of Soveraign no more given by the Grantees to him that Grants them, the Grant is voyd:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any apparent grant of sovereign privileges is void unless the sovereign explicitly renounces the sovereignty itself; formal retention of sovereign status preserves the rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence Of Sovereign Annihilates Subjects' Power And Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: This great Authority being indivisible, ... the Power And Honour Of Subjects Vanisheth In The Presence Of The Power Soveraign ... in his presence, they shine no more than the Starres in presence of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes stresses symbolic and practical supremacy of sovereign: subjects' individual power and honour are eclipsed in sovereign presence because honour and dignity flow from the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Power Less Harmful Than Want Of It (Defense Of Absolutism)
rubrics_metrics.description: the greatest ... that in any forme of Government can possibly happen to the people in generall, is scarce sensible, in respect of the miseries, and horrible calamities, that accompany a Civill Warre; or that dissolute condition of masterlesse men, without subjection to Lawes, and a coercive Power ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that the inconveniences of absolute sovereign power are minor compared to chaos of civil war; justification for strong, even unlimited, sovereign authority as necessary to avoid worse evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Three Kinds Of Common-wealth (Classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference of Common-wealths, consisteth in the difference of the Soveraign ... there can be but Three kinds of Common-wealth ... MONARCHY (one man), DEMOCRACY (assembly of all that will come), ARISTOCRACY (assembly of a part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a typology for states based on who bears the sovereign person. Hobbes maintains that these exhaust the possible legitimate arrangements because the representative must be one, more, or all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate Representatives Are Dangerous / No Two Sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore, where there is already erected a Soveraign Power, there can be no other Representative of the same people, but onely to certain particular ends, by the Soveraigne limited. For that were to erect two Soveraignes; ... And therefore as it is absurd, to think that a Soveraigne Assembly, inviting the People ... should therefore hold such Deputies ... for the absolute Representative of the people:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against parallel or competing representations: establishing multiple sovereign representatives divides the person of the commonwealth and risks returning to war. Any subsidiary representation must be limited by the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Criteria For Evaluating Forms (Monarchy vs Assemblies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between these three kindes of Common-wealth, consisteth not in the difference of Power; but in the difference of Convenience, or Aptitude to produce the Peace, and Security of the people ... followed by comparative points: unity of public/private interest in monarchy, counsel selection and secrecy, greater constancy of monarchic resolution, assemblies may disagree with themselves, danger of favourites and corruption in both, problem of infant succession and need for regency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists practical evaluative criteria for choosing between monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy: which form better secures peace, allows timely and secret counsel, avoids factional inconstancy, and handles succession. Hobbes argues monarchy often has practical advantages (united interest, secrecy, constancy) though it has particular drawbacks (favourites, regency).
